title: Where Do the Two Lists Meet?

concept.title: Walk both lists and swap at the end
body: Two lists may **merge**: from some node on, they are the **same nodes** (not just equal values). Their last nodes are shared, so from the merging node to the end both lists have the same length. If list A has `a` nodes before the merging point, list B has `b`, and the shared part has `c` nodes, then A has length `a + c` and B has `b + c`.

Use two references, `p` on A and `q` on B. When one reaches the end, it **jumps to the head of the other list**. Then `p` walks `a + c + b` nodes and `q` walks `b + c + a` nodes in total: the same number. So after at most that many steps they stand on the merging node together. If the lists do not merge, both become `None` at the same moment and the loop ends.

body.code:
p, q = head_a, head_b
while p is not q:
    p = p.next if p is not None else head_b
    q = q.next if q is not None else head_a
return p            # the merging node, or None

body: The comparison must be about **node identity** (`is` in Python, `==` on pointers in C++ and Java), not about the values. The starter builds the two lists so that they share their last `c` nodes, and prints how many nodes there are from the returned node to the end.

statement: Two singly linked lists share their last `c` nodes (the very same nodes). List A consists of its own `a` nodes followed by the shared nodes, list B of its own `b` nodes followed by the same shared nodes. Find the first shared node, and print the number of nodes from it to the end of the list (this is `c`, and 0 if `c = 0` and the lists do not meet).
inputFormat: The second line has the values of the own nodes of A.
The third line has the values of the own nodes of B.
The fourth line has the values of the shared nodes. A line is empty when its count is 0.
outputFormat: Print the number of nodes from the first shared node to the end, or 0.
constraints: -10^9 <= each value <= 10^9 (values may repeat, also between the lists)

examples.note: A is 4 1 8 4 and B is 5 6 1 8 4; they meet at 8: 2 nodes remain.

hints: Equal values do not mean the same node: compare the nodes themselves.
Move two references; when one falls off the end, send it to the head of the other list.
After both have walked both lists, they meet at the shared node or both become empty.

# Every node is also remembered in this list. Python in the browser cannot free a very long chain of nodes at once,
# so free_nodes() (called at the end) cuts the links first and the nodes are then freed one by one.
all_nodes = []


class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next
        all_nodes.append(self)


def free_nodes():
    for node in all_nodes:
        node.next = None
        if hasattr(node, "random"):
            node.random = None
    all_nodes.clear()


# Builds a list from the values. If pos is 0 or more, the last node points back to the node at index pos (a cycle).
def build_list(values, pos=-1):
    head = None
    for v in reversed(values):
        head = ListNode(v, head)
    if pos >= 0:
        tail = head
        while tail.next is not None:
            tail = tail.next
        target = head
        for _ in range(pos):
            target = target.next
        tail.next = target
    return head


# Prints the values of a list on one line ("empty" for an empty list).

    out = []
    while head is not None:
        out.append(head.val)
        head = head.next
    print(*(out if out else ["empty"]))

explanation: Each reference walks its own list and then the other one, so both walk `a + b + c` nodes and meet at the first shared node, or become empty together if there is none.
solution.complexity: Time O(a + b + c), space O(1).
